name: Orbital Resonance
statement: When orbits fall into whole-number ratios, bodies tug each other in rhythm, locking or clearing them.
statementAccent: bodies tug each other in rhythm, locking or clearing them
meaning: Orbital resonance occurs when two or more orbiting bodies exert a regular, periodic gravitational influence on one another, usually because their orbital periods are related by a ratio of small whole numbers, such as two to one or three to two. When periods are commensurate in this way, the bodies repeatedly line up in the same relative positions, so their mutual gravitational tugs accumulate rather than averaging out. The most common form is the mean-motion resonance, in which the orbital periods themselves stand in an integer ratio. Resonance can have opposite effects: in some cases it locks bodies into remarkably stable configurations that persist for the age of the solar system, while in others it pumps up eccentricities and destabilizes orbits, clearing gaps or ejecting objects. This dual character makes orbital resonance a powerful sculptor of planetary systems, responsible for the stable dance of the Galilean moons, the gaps in the asteroid belt, and structure in planetary rings, and a key to reading the history of how systems formed and migrated.
mechanism: Resonance arises because commensurate orbital periods make gravitational interactions repeat in phase. If two bodies have periods in a simple ratio, they return to the same relative geometry again and again, so the small gravitational nudge one gives the other at a particular point in the orbit is repeated in the same direction each cycle, and these nudges add up instead of cancelling. The result depends on the configuration. In a protective, stable resonance, the geometry is arranged so the bodies never make their closest approaches where they would most disturb each other, and the resonance actually shepherds and preserves the orbits, as with Neptune and Pluto, locked in a three-to-two resonance that keeps them far apart despite crossing paths. In a destabilizing resonance, the repeated tugs steadily increase a body's eccentricity until its orbit changes drastically or it is ejected, which clears the Kirkwood gaps in the asteroid belt at resonances with Jupiter and opens divisions in Saturn's rings. The three Galilean moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede share a linked one-two-four Laplace resonance.

examples.text: Jupiter's moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede orbit in a linked one-two-four resonance, a stable chain in which their periods are commensurate.
Pluto orbits in a three-to-two resonance with Neptune that keeps the two far apart at crossing points, stabilizing Pluto's orbit.
Resonances with Jupiter clear gaps in the asteroid belt at ratios like three-to-one and five-to-two, and open divisions in Saturn's rings.

variants.name: Stabilizing resonance
variants.text: A configuration, like the Laplace resonance or Neptune-Pluto, in which the repeated tugs shepherd and preserve the orbits.

variants.name: Destabilizing resonance
variants.text: A configuration in which repeated tugs pump up eccentricity and clear objects, as at the Kirkwood gaps and ring divisions.

whyItMatters: Orbital resonance is a fundamental organizing force in planetary systems, shaping their architecture, ring structure, and small-body populations, and recording their history. Stable resonances lock moons and planets into enduring configurations, from the Galilean moons' Laplace resonance to the Neptune-Pluto lock and the resonant chains of exoplanets like the seven worlds of TRAPPIST-1, while destabilizing resonances sculpt the asteroid belt into the Kirkwood gaps and carve divisions in Saturn's rings. Because resonances are so sensitive to orbital periods, their presence is evidence of how systems formed and evolved: resonant chains in particular are thought to arise as planets migrate through the gas of a young disk and become captured, so finding them constrains theories of planet formation and migration. Resonance thus links the everyday spectacle of moons and rings to deep questions about the origin of planetary systems.

working.text: have two or more bodies whose orbital periods stand in a ratio of small whole numbers.
let the repeated relative geometry make gravitational nudges add up in phase rather than cancelling.
depending on configuration, either shepherd the orbits into a stable lock or pump eccentricity until objects are cleared.

limits: Orbital resonance can stabilize or destabilize depending on the precise configuration, so the presence of a small-integer period ratio alone does not tell you which will happen; the geometry of closest approaches and the phase of the resonance determine the outcome. Whether a resonance holds also depends on the masses involved and the strength of the interaction, and resonances can be temporary, captured and later broken as orbits evolve. The Kirkwood gaps and ring divisions arise from specific resonances with major perturbers, not from resonance in general. Some resonant chains, like TRAPPIST-1, are near-resonant rather than exactly commensurate. So orbital resonance is a powerful and pervasive influence on orbits, but its effect, stabilizing or destabilizing, depends on the detailed configuration rather than following automatically from a period ratio.
misreadings: Orbital resonance is not always destabilizing or always stabilizing; the same phenomenon locks the Galilean moons into a stable chain and clears the Kirkwood gaps, depending on the configuration. A small-integer period ratio does not by itself guarantee a stable lock, since the geometry of encounters decides the outcome. And resonance is not a rare curiosity but a widespread sculptor of systems, so treating resonance as inherently good or bad for orbits, or as merely coincidental, misreads a phenomenon whose amplified, in-phase gravitational tugs can either preserve or destroy orbits according to the arrangement.
origin: A phenomenon of celestial mechanics in which orbiting bodies with commensurate periods exert repeated, accumulating gravitational influence, long studied through the moons, rings, and asteroid gaps of the solar system.
